Top 5 Strongest

At each week’s last close (usually Friday), rank the S&P 500 by 6-month performance (skipping the latest month), hold the 5 strongest that beat SPY, and keep each while it stays in the top 10. Trade at the next session (usually Monday), 3:30–4:00 pm ET.

In plain words: the latest news is “S&P 500 −4.2% in a day: Asian markets split after the US midterms: AI/chip stocks sold off hard in Japan and South Korea while Hong Kong rallied on hopes a Democratic-led Congress could ease tariffs. (news log)”. After the 9 past Trade war / China events, stocks (the S&P 500) were higher 3 months later more often than usual (89% of the time, against 69% normally). Of the 2 news items in the last month, 1 usually came before weaker stocks than normal and 1 before stronger. These are tendencies, not forecasts, and the plan does not trade on them.

A few held up: fear spikes (VIX over 40) were followed by a higher S&P 500 3 months later 7 times in 8, Fed and government rescues by a higher S&P 500 a month later 9 in 10, and wars by lower oil a month later 7 in 10. The plan doesn't use this.

History, not a forecast. Tested from 2000 (316 month-ends, each matched only with earlier days), these matches ranked the months before a 10%+ fall no better than a coin flip (52%, where 50% is chance) and scored worse than the normal rate; the domino count alone did better (63%). Acting on the dominoes cost the plan: stepping out of stocks on them made 20–26% a year from 2000 against the plan's 45.8% (research, Oct 2026). Information only: the plan doesn't use this.

Where hedge funds and other speculators sit in each futures market, against their own last 3 years: 0% = the most short they have been, 100% = the most long. The shaded ends are the top and bottom 10%, crowded. ▲▼ = change since the week before.

  • Crowded long has not been a reliable sell warning. Since 2000 a 10%+ fall within 2 months followed more often than usual only in silver (33% of crowded weeks, 24% normally) and S&P 500 futures (28% against 11%, few cases), not in gold, copper, oil or Nasdaq-100 futures. It also missed the May–June 2006 metals crash.
  • Crowded short in stock futures has been a good sign for stocks. The S&P 500 was higher 3 months later 79% of the time (+5.1% on average, against +2.4% normally).
  • Neither works as a trading rule: tested on the plan, stepping out when crowded long or into the index when crowded short both did worse. A heads-up on positioning, not a timing signal; it changes nothing the plan does.

    Plan = Boost + rotation (surge exit, whipsaw switch (the whole account into TLT or GLD) with the rate/gold regime, TLT / GLD by 6-month gain, narrow-market cash week read from the equal-weight index’s full history, lower-high exit into gold or bonds on both its triggers, no T-bills: gold or bonds if up over 3 months, else DBMF managed futures (from its start in May 2019; cash before); price-break rule: the day SPY closes under its 100-day average for the first time with that average and its 7-day average both falling, the haven pick for 10 sessions; buy freeze: no new stocks for 10 sessions after a week ends with SPY within 1% of a weekly lower high that the daily chart confirms, an empty slot in the haven pick; green light: weekly and daily higher lows lift the buy filters and skip the cash week for 10 sessions; rebound rule: stays in stocks after a 12%+ drop with gold or bonds up 2%+ and a daily higher low; break re-entry rule: after a 10%+ drop, a weekly and a daily downtrend break (the daily one on fading volume) within 21 sessions hold stocks for 21 sessions; fading-energy filter: a top-5 stock whose volume and daily swings have both faded isn’t bought, its slot stays in cash; the whipsaw check counts the list with the filter off; buying-volume weighting: at each trade a held stock in the top third of the S&P 500 by up-day vs down-day volume over 3 months gets twice the money of the others; earnings-jump weighting: a held stock that closed 3%+ higher on its last earnings report within 3 months gets twice its money too; stretched-and-warned exit: when 3 or more of the eight dominoes are down and SPY is 2+ standard errors above its 52-week trend line, the haven for 20 sessions; near-the-high weighting: a held stock within 3% of its 1-year high gets twice its money too, no stock above 40% of the account; hot-commodity buy skip: no new metals or energy buy while copper or oil is up 50%+ over 6 months; unemployment step-aside: when the unemployment rate has climbed 0.3 points from its low of the year before while SPY is under its 150-day average, the haven for 21 sessions; the near-the-high doubling off while SPY is under its 150-day average; heavy-volume selling: no new buy within 5 sessions of a down close on 4x+ the 50-day average volume, and a holding that closes 6%+ down on 4x+ volume is sold, the sell only while SPY is above its 150-day average; rule order: the break re-entry wins over the unemployment step-aside, the lower-high exit over the rebound rule; candle re-entry: after a 12%+ drop, two red days making a fresh 20-day low and then a close above both of their opens hold stocks for 10 sessions over the other rules, but not once SPY is more than 30% under its high; run-up skip: while SPY is down over 6 months, no new buy of a stock up 50%+ in 2 months; no stock above 50% of the account; crash-rebound ranking: within 6 months of SPY closing 30%+ under its 1-year high, while SPY is above its 50-day average, the 10 most volatile, deepest-under-their-high, lowest-priced stocks are ranked first). Previous plan = the same plan without the crash-rebound ranking (until Nov 9, 2026). From the audit’s daily curves: stocks in the S&P 500 at the time, from the real daily member lists (since Oct 26, 2026; before, lists rebuilt from Wikipedia’s change table held companies years before they joined), with prices for former members from Tiingo (a few series that belonged to other companies left out); 0.15% slippage, 37%/20% tax; Sharpe and Sortino net of a 2% cash rate. EP and CPWR are left out (their tickers were reused by later companies).

    Back to the peak how long the plan took to get back to a previous high · every drop of 15% or more · daily closes from Jan 2000

For comparison, SPY waited 79 months (Mar 2000 to Oct 2006). QQQ waited 179 months (Mar 2000 to Feb 2015).     • Overfitting test (PBO, 1388 versions): a 2.3% chance that the best-looking version is a fluke, judged on years it was not picked on. Under 50% means picking the best version helped.
    • Deflated Sharpe ratio (1,388 versions): a 99.69% chance the edge is real after allowing for how many versions were tried. Luck alone would give the best of that many versions a Sharpe ratio of about 0.79; the plan’s is 1.31. Above 95% is the usual bar.
    • Walk-forward: re-picking the best version each year, using only the years before it, earned 32.9% a year in 2005–2025 against 23.6% for the typical version.
    • The same tests among close versions only (324 versions of the current plan tried on the real member lists, 2026-11-02: every rule switched off in turn and every variation tested that day): the deflated Sharpe ratio is still 100% (luck alone would give about 0.2–0.55; the plan’s is 1.46), so the edge over doing nothing is real. But the overfitting test is 51% (56% among the 295 within 10 points of the best), and re-picking the best version each year made 45.3% a year in 2005–2026 against 45.9–46.2% for the typical one: picking between close versions is a coin flip, so each small rule added on probation is not proven by the backtest and is judged on the paper record.
    • The narrow-market cash week on its own: about 5.6 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 1.9 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 45.9%, 55.7% vs 46.8% from 2010, 73.2% vs 58.9% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 85.4% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −32%. Month by month the gain is not proven (most months it does nothing); judged on its cash weeks against random weeks it is unlikely to be luck. It was found on 2012–2026, went 1 for 3 on the 2006–07 years it was not built on, and did not carry over abroad (below), so it is on probation.
    • The rebound rule on its own: about 1.7 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 0.9 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 49.8%, 55.7% vs 54.0% from 2010, 73.2% vs 72.2% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 106.6% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −27%. Month by month the gain is not proven; it rests on a handful of bear-market bottoms (most of it late October 2008) and was picked after many timing tests, so it is on probation.
    • The fading-energy filter on its own: about 2.8 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 1.4 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 48.6%, 55.7% vs 52.8% from 2010, 73.2% vs 68.9% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 104.0% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −26%. It was found by studying the plan's own losing picks, so it is on probation.
    • The lower-high exit on its own: about 3.9 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 1.7 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 47.5%, 55.7% vs 51.0% from 2010, 73.2% vs 67.6% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 97.7% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −32%. Month by month the gain is not proven (most months it does nothing); the point is the smaller drops. It was designed after looking at the 2007–2011 and 2022 drops, so it is on probation.
    • No T-bills on its own (gold or bonds if up over 6 months, else cash; 3 months since Oct 19, 2026; DBMF managed futures instead of cash since Oct 20, 2026): about 4.3 points a year over T-bills on the real member lists (Nov 2, 2026: 51.4% vs 47.1% from 2000, 106.6% vs 93.5% from 2020, t-stat 2.9); earlier, about 3.1 points a year over T-bills (t-stat 3.1 on monthly returns) and about 3.4 over plain cash; it beat the T-bills version in 92/98/100% of simulated 5 / 10 / 20-year futures and plain cash in 93/99/100% (measured on the old member lists). The gain is lumpy (bonds in late 2008, gold in the 2024–2025 cash weeks; gold cost about 40 points of 2026's gain), so count on it doing about as well as T-bills.
    • The 3-month look on its own (gold or bonds by their 3-month gain instead of 6, wherever the plan would hold T-bills; default since Oct 19, 2026): about 0.9 points a year over the 6-month pick (t-stat 1.2 on monthly returns): 42.4% a year from 2000 vs 41.0%, ahead from all seven start years tested (by 1.3 to 2.8 points) and in 232 of 285 rolling 3-year windows; it beat the 6-month version in 71/80/88% of simulated 5 / 10 / 20-year futures; 2013–2025 about level, so 2026 carries much of the recent gain; in Japan, the UK and Germany it was about half a point a year better (measured before the price-break rule) (measured on the old member lists). Most of the gain is a few stretches (2026, 2009, 2017) and it cost 15 points in 2025, so it is on probation.
    • Managed futures instead of cash on its own (DBMF, a fund that follows trends in stock, bond, currency and commodity futures, wherever the no-T-bills pick finds neither gold nor bonds up; default since Oct 20, 2026): about 1.1 points a year over the plan with plain cash from 2000 (t-stat 2.1 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 50.3%, 55.7% vs 53.8% from 2010, 73.2% vs 70.0% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 100.6% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −27%. The fund began in May 2019, so the gain is from then on; it rests on a few stretches and is on probation.
    • The 6-month pick on its own: adds about 0.5 points a year, t 0.8 (measured on the old member lists); a t-stat under 2 means the gain is not proven, so it is on probation.
    • Other countries (the same rules on each market's own stocks, without the cash week): Japan 18.9%, UK 12.6%, Germany 8.5%, India 34.1%, Hong Kong 28.1% a year (6.7%, 2.0%, 5.4%, 14.1%, 2.5% for their indexes).
    • The cash week abroad (rebuilt with an equal-weight basket of each index's current stocks and the US VIX or the index's own volatility; on US data these stand-ins kept most of the gain): Japan 18.9% a year without it vs 16.7–17.8% with it, UK 12.6% vs 12.4–12.6%, Germany 8.5% vs 6.5–6.7%, Hong Kong 28.1% vs 27.0–27.5%, India 34.1% vs 32.7–35.1%. It fired less often abroad and, in Germany and Japan, at the wrong times, so it looks specific to the US since 2012.
    • Before the data it was built on: 15.0% a year in 1927–1999 against 10.7% for the market (top 10% momentum, trend filter, monthly).
    • What to plan on: about 25% a year before tax, the low end of the 24–34% the latest overfitting test points to (most of the newer versions are small changes to the best plan, which flatters the test). The rules were picked on the same history they are tested on, so the headline numbers are the best case.
    • The price-break rule on its own: about 2.3 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 1.9 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 49.2%, 55.7% vs 54.5% from 2010, 73.2% vs 71.7% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 104.7% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −28%. It rests on a handful of breaks (99 haven days in 27 years) and one idea tried many ways, so it is on probation.
    • The buy freeze and green light on their own (default since Oct 26, 2026): about 0.1 points a year over the plan without the buy freeze from 2000 (t-stat 0.1 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 51.3%, 55.7% vs 55.1% from 2010, 73.2% vs 72.7% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 106.9% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −31%; and 1.1 over the plan without the green light (50.3%, t-stat 1.1). A coin flip on the history, so they are on probation; the paper record decides.
    • The break re-entry rule on its own (default since Oct 27, 2026): about 1.5 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 1.4 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 50.0%, 55.7% vs 53.8% from 2010, 73.2% vs 69.3% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 99.4% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −27%. It rests on 7 trades and was shaped after seeing a failure on the same history (the daily break alone bought back in two weeks before Lehman), so it is on probation.
    • The whipsaw switch without SPY on its own (TLT or GLD only, else DBMF or cash; default since Oct 28, 2026): about level with the plan with SPY as a third choice from 2000 (t-stat 1.0 on monthly returns, real member lists): 40.4% a year from 2000 vs 40.3%, 44.3% vs 44.5% from 2010, 59.5% vs 58.7% from 2016 and 70.1% vs 70.1% from 2020, the same worst drops. It rests on a few stretches and is too small to call proven, so it is on probation.
    • The Fed-day hold on its own (a move out of stocks waits one session when its trade would land just before a scheduled Fed decision day; default since Oct 31, 2026): about 0.5 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 1.6 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 51.0%, 55.7% vs 55.3% from 2010, 73.2% vs 72.9% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 105.7% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −28%. It acted 6 times in 26 years, so it is on probation.
    • The buying-volume weighting on its own (twice the money for a held stock whose up-day volume over down-day volume is in the top third of the S&P 500; default since Nov 2, 2026): ahead of equal weights from every start (real member lists): 42.7% a year from 2000 vs 40.7%, 47.0% vs 45.5% from 2010, 60.0% vs 57.8% from 2016 and 86.6% vs 83.8% from 2020, worst drop -34% vs -35%, Sharpe 1.30 vs 1.26, still ahead at 0.30% a side (34.1% vs 32.7%); with the later Nov 2 rules added, 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 45.0%, 55.7% vs 49.1% from 2010, 73.2% vs 63.5% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 90.6% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −33% (t-stat 3.0). It held at every nearby setting tested but did not show up in eight foreign markets, so it is on probation.
    • The earnings-jump weighting on its own (twice the money for a held stock that jumped 3%+ on its last earnings report within 3 months; default since Nov 2, 2026): ahead of the plan without it from every start (t-stat 2.3 on monthly returns, real member lists): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 49.1%, 55.7% vs 52.5% from 2010, 73.2% vs 68.4% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 98.0% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −28%. Nearly all the gain came in 2016–2026, so it is on probation.
    • The stretched-and-warned exit on its own (the haven for 20 sessions when 3+ dominoes are down and SPY is stretched 2+ standard errors above its 52-week trend line; default since Nov 2, 2026): about 1.1 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 1.4 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 50.3%, the same from 2001 on; worst drop −27% vs −35%; it acted only once since 2000 (Mar 24, 2000, the dot-com top), and its trend-line setting sits just under SPY's stretch that day. One trade caught by a line set after seeing it, so it is on probation.
    • The third Nov 2 change on its own (the near-the-high weighting with a 40% cap, the hot-commodity buy skip and the unemployment step-aside; default since Nov 2, 2026): the three rules of the third Nov 2 change together (with a 40% cap on any one stock): about 1.8 points a year over the plan without them from 2000 (t-stat 0.9 on monthly returns, real member lists): 47.6% a year from 2000 vs 45.8%, 52.0% vs 49.4% from 2010, 67.9% vs 64.7% from 2016 and 102.0% vs 94.9% from 2020; worst drop −28% vs −33%; ahead in 14 years and behind in 13, each setting the best of a search, and nearby settings fell behind from 2016 and 2020. On probation.
    • The near-the-high doubling off in a down market on its own (no 2× for a stock near its high while SPY is under its 150-day average; default since Nov 2, 2026): about 0.7 points a year over the plan with the doubling always on from 2000 (t-stat 1.4 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 2, 2026): 48.2% a year from 2000 vs 47.6%, 52.6% vs 52.0% from 2010, 69.1% vs 67.9% from 2016 and 103.6% vs 102.0% from 2020; worst drop −28% either way; ahead in 12 years and behind in 7, with 2000 and 2025 carrying most of the gain. The 100- and 200-day averages gave about the same, but the gain is not proven, so it is on probation.
    • Heavy-volume selling on its own (no new buy within 5 sessions of a down close on 4× volume, and a holding that closes 6%+ down on 4× volume is sold; default since Nov 3, 2026): about 1.8 points a year over the plan without it from 2000 (t-stat 1.2 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 3, 2026): 50.0% a year from 2000 vs 48.2%, 53.6% vs 52.6% from 2010, 71.0% vs 69.1% from 2016 and 104.4% vs 103.6% from 2020; worst drop −27% vs −28%; ahead in 14 years and behind in 10; 10 of 12 nearby settings ahead from 2000, but a few trades in 2005, 2007, 2013 and 2025 carry it and it was the best of 30 combinations tried; since Nov 3, 2026 its sell part acts only while SPY is above its 150-day average: 50.5% a year from 2000 vs 50.0% with the sell in any market, 105.1% vs 104.4% from 2020, the same worst drop (t-stat 0.6; the 100- and 200-day averages agreed). On probation.
    • The rule order on its own (the break re-entry wins over the unemployment step-aside, the lower-high exit over the rebound rule; default since Nov 3, 2026): about 0.9 points a year over the rules in the order they were added, from 2000 (t-stat 1.9 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 3, 2026): 51.4% a year from 2000 vs 50.5%, 55.7% vs 55.1% from 2010, 73.2% vs 72.4% from 2016 and 106.6% vs 105.1% from 2020; worst drop −27% either way; better in 4 years (2020 +12.9, 2008 +9.0, 2002 +5.6, 2011 +1.0 points) and worse in none, so it rests on few years. On probation.
    • The candle re-entry rule on its own (after a deep drop, two down days at a fresh low and then a day that undoes them put the plan in stocks for two weeks over the other rules; default since Nov 5, 2026): about 1.2 points a year over the plan without it, from 2000 (t-stat 1.0 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 5, 2026): 52.6% a year from 2000 vs 51.4%, 57.5% vs 55.7% from 2010, 75.4% vs 73.2% from 2016 and 110.8% vs 106.6% from 2020; worst drop −26% vs −27%; better in 6 years and worse in 2; 20 of 27 nearby settings ahead from every start; it fired 20 times in 26 years and October 2022 carries most of the gain. On probation.
    • The run-up skip on its own (while the market is falling, no new buy of a stock that has just shot up; default since Nov 6, 2026): about 1.5 points a year over the plan without it, from 2000 (t-stat 1.8 on monthly returns, real member lists, Nov 6, 2026): 54.1% a year from 2000 vs 52.6%, 58.5% vs 57.5% from 2010, 77.1% vs 75.4% from 2016 and 114.1% vs 110.8% from 2020; the same −26% worst drop; better in 6 years and worse in 1; all 8 nearby versions with a 40–50% run over 2 months ahead from every start; most of the gain is in 2003, 2026 and 2002. On probation.
    • The candle re-entry rule’s 30% cap (rule 19 no longer acts once the market has fallen more than 30%, a crash; since Nov 7, 2026): replayed abroad (UK, Germany, France, Canada, Australia and Hong Kong, 2005–2026, today's index members, the local index in place of SPY) the candle re-entry rule cost points in all six markets, mostly by buying back in during the 2008 crash 30–50% down; of 9 stricter versions only the 30% cap was ahead both in the US and abroad: 54.3% a year from 2000 vs 54.1%, the same from 2010, 2016 and 2020, the same −26% worst drop (it skips Jul 2002 and Mar 24, 2020; 2002 gains 3.7 points), and abroad +0.5 points a year on average, ahead in 4 markets and behind in none; abroad the rule is still about 0.7 points a year worse than none (Nov 7, 2026). Still on probation.
    • The 50% cap per stock (no stock above half the account, up from 40%; since Nov 7, 2026): the per-stock cap raised from 40% to 50% (Nov 7, 2026): 54.9% a year from 2000 vs 54.3%, 59.4% vs 58.5% from 2010, 79.0% vs 77.1% from 2016 and 116.7% vs 114.1% from 2020, worst drop −25% vs −26%, ahead in 16 years and behind in 10 (t-stat 1.7); no cap made the same 54.9% but let one stock reach 62% of the account; caps of 25–38% all lost (51.4–54.0%) and made 2006 worse; most of the gain is in 2021 and 2025. On probation.
    • The crash-rebound ranking on its own (after a 30%+ crash, once the market turns up, the stocks most likely to rebound ranked first; default since Nov 9, 2026): after a 30%+ crash, once SPY is back above its 50-day average, the stocks most likely to rebound ranked first (Nov 9, 2026): 60.4% a year from 2000 vs 54.9%, 61.9% vs 59.4% from 2010, 82.0% vs 79.0% from 2016 and 122.5% vs 116.7% from 2020, the same −25% worst drop, better in 5 years and worse in 1 (2002), t-stat 1.5; it was on about 8% of the time (late 2001–2003, the 2009 rebound, spring–summer 2020); without the wait for SPY to turn up it bought into falling markets (worst drop −35% to −45%); abroad, with its times doubled on a 12-month look-back, +0.9 points a year in 9 markets, better in 5 and worse in 1; most of the gain is in 2003, 2009 and 2020. On probation.

Replayed walk-forward 2012–2026 on 13 markets it kept the S&P 500 on the full plan every year, sent thin markets (UK, Germany, France, Canada, Australia, Spain, Italy, Sweden) to the 12-month pick and kept the Russell 2000 on its index: 24.6% a year on average vs 11.0% for the index, ahead of the index in 12 of 13. Reviews more often than yearly switched 3–10 times as often and did worse. Reviewed in January by the track-record refresh.       Five-year winners & early signals research · Oct 2021 – Oct 2026 · prices from Yahoo Finance to the 2026-10-09 close

      AI suppliers won, and most of them flagged themselves with one huge-volume day

      The biggest US winners of the last five years were mostly not the famous AI names but the companies selling the "picks and shovels" of the data-center build-out: servers, switchgear, cooling, optics, memory and power. Almost every durable move started with a quantified demand surprise (guidance far above consensus, a tripled backlog, a gigawatt-scale contract, a first profit) and a single ignition day: a big gap up on several times normal volume, usually closing at a new 52-week high.

      Start date matters. Stocks that crashed in 2022 look ordinary over five years but were the biggest winners from the low: Carvana +8,466% (after −99%), AppLovin +2,879% (after −92%), Palantir +3,384%, Robinhood +1,482%. Small-cap trough-to-peak moves were bigger still: Rigetti ~150x, Sezzle ~139x, GeneDx ~135x, D-Wave ~108x.

      Many started as mid caps (CLS, STRL, FIX, BE, LITE, CRDO, POWL) and only later became large caps, so a scan limited to today's index members misses them early. Celestica trades on the NYSE and is not in the S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100.

      Why they shot up: guidance shocks tied to a capex cycle
      • NVIDIA guided ~$11B vs ~$7.2B expected (May 2023) → +24% next day.
      • Broadcom sized its AI market at $60–90B for FY2027 (Dec 2024) → +24%, passed $1T.
      • Powell reported backlog nearly tripled to a record $1.3B (Aug 2023), before the data-center story attached to it.
      • Credo guided $115–125M off a much smaller base → +48% in a day.
      • Constellation signed the 20-year Microsoft deal to restart Three Mile Island → +22%. Bloom signed up to 1 GW with AEP → +59%.
      • Turnarounds ignited on first profits or debt fixes: Carvana (positive EBITDA guide, ~50% of float short), Sezzle (Q1 2024 profit beat all of 2023), Root (revenue +173%).

      What held vs. what round-tripped. All 16 theme stocks checked (quantum, small nuclear, space, eVTOL, speculative AI) are now 47–87% below their peaks; several had little or no revenue when they spiked. About 10 of 15 backlog-and-earnings compounders are within ~40% of their highs. Earnings alone weren't enough: Celsius, Duolingo, Cava and Hims still fell 55–72% when growth slowed. The durable recipe: revenue already accelerating, a multi-year backlog, and demand tied to a measurable spending cycle, confirmed again every quarter.

      Skeptics were still around after ignition (Palantir kept Hold/Sell ratings), and S&P 500 inclusion acted as a later accelerant (APP +11.6%, HOOD +15.8% the next session).

      • Ignitions cluster. In NVIDIA's May 2023 report week, Broadcom and Vertiv also broke out on heavy volume. Waves: AI hardware (Feb–Aug 2023), power (2024), post-election (Nov–Dec 2024), memory (Apr–Sep 2025). When a leader posts a blowout, scan its suppliers next.
      • The first ignition often isn't the one that pays. Micron (Dec 2023) and Dell went nowhere for a year with ~60% drawdowns before their real leg. The big trends came from repeated earnings gap-ups: Powell, AppLovin, Credo and Sezzle each had three to six.
      • Small caps were more extreme: 20–75% days on 5–85x volume (Root 85x, GeneDx 35x, AST SpaceMobile 22x).
      Reality check: base rates and hindsight
      • Most stocks lose. About 4% of US stocks account for all the market's net gain over T-bills since 1926 (Bessembinder). Roughly 0.7–2% of stocks go 10x in 10 years.
      • Traits barely predict it. Observable characteristics explain only ~2% of which stocks become decade-long winners.
      • The proven signals give modest edges: momentum (~5.5%/yr after publication), nearness to the 52-week high (George & Hwang), the high-volume return premium (Gervais, Kaniel & Mingelgrin), earnings-day volume plus surprise. Classic post-earnings drift has largely vanished from liquid US stocks since ~2006.
      • Volume alone makes breakouts less reliable. In Bulkowski's ~8,000-pattern study, heavy-volume breakouts failed 14% vs 5% for quiet ones and pulled back to the breakout 57% vs 18% of the time.
      • Failures look identical at ignition. Super Micro's Jan 2024 day (+36%, 7.3x volume, new high) was the perfect signature; it then fell 85% after a short report and its auditor resigning.
      • This study is hindsight too: the 23 ignitions were picked because they worked. How many lookalike days led nowhere was not measured.
      How to catch the next ones: scan rules
      #RuleDefinition (daily OHLCV)
      1Wide universeInclude NYSE / NYSE American names outside the big indexes; price ≥ $5, 50-day dollar volume ≥ ~$5–20M
      2Up-day qualityUp day closing in the top 40% of its range: (C−L)/(H−L) ≥ 0.6. Treat down-day volume spikes as distribution, not signals
      3Ignition gapOpen ≥ 8% above prior close on ≥ 3x 50-day average volume, holding (close ≥ open or upper half of range)
      4Trend gateC > SMA50 > SMA150 > SMA200, SMA200 rising over 21 sessions, within 25% of the 52-week high and ≥ 25% above the low; bonus for a new 252-day high
      5Relative strength0.4·r63 + 0.2·each earlier quarter, percentile ≥ 80; bonus when the stock/SPY line hits a 52-week high before price
      6Repeat & groupBoost names with ≥ 2 qualifying gaps in 12 months, and names whose industry peers flagged within 5 sessions
      7Pocket pivotUp-day volume above the largest down-day volume of the prior 10 sessions: quieter accumulation before the gap
      8Calendar hygieneDiscount opex, triple witching / S&P rebalance Fridays, Russell reconstitution and index-add days (mechanical volume)

      Turnaround lane. Palantir, AppLovin, Vistra and Carvana ignited 20–72% below their highs, so the trend gate rejects them. Track them separately: ≥ 15% gap on ≥ 5x volume with strong 3-month relative strength. Expect more volatility.

      Rank on a composite (setup flags, RS percentile, nearness to the high, then volume ratio), not on raw volume ratio. Then backtest the flags over 2015–2026 to get their real hit and failure rates before sizing anything.

      Playbook: many small bets, re-enter second legs

      Nearly every winner bottomed near 2025-04-04 (Vertiv −61%, Credo −61%, AppLovin −57%, Celestica −54%). A fixed −20% stop would have shaken you out of almost all of them. Pick one style:

      • Swing: buy the ignition close or next day's opening range; stop at the gap-day low; take ⅓–½ off near +20%; trail the rest on the 10/20-day average; risk ~0.5–1% of equity per trade.
      • Compounder: admit only names with accelerating revenue, growing backlog or rising margins; start small enough to survive a 50–60% drawdown; add on the 2nd and 3rd earnings gaps; exit on a broken thesis (guidance cut, accounting/auditor event, lost customer), not price alone.
      1. Hold many small, roughly equal positions; winners are rare and skewed.
      2. Re-enter names that re-ignite; Micron and Dell paid on the second ignition.
      3. Cut new-entry size after big market drawdowns; momentum crashes in panic rebounds.
      4. Exit a theme when several peers post high-volume down days together (quantum and nuclear peaked together Oct 7–15, 2025).
      5. Short interest and options flow: tie-breakers only.

      Research summary, not investment advice. Returns are split-adjusted closes from Yahoo Finance; figures after ~June 2026 rest on price data alone. Full report with sources: Five year stock winners and early signals.

      • The rule. Score = return from 6 months ago to 1 month ago. Each Friday close: a stock must beat SPY's score to qualify; buy the top 5 in equal weight; a holding stays while it ranks in the top 10, otherwise it is replaced by the best-ranked stock not held. Trades are placed the following Monday in the last 30 minutes before the close (the track record uses Monday's closing prices; trading at Monday's open did about 3% a year worse in testing). Mon–Thu the banner previews what Friday's signal would be if it were today.
      • Fair test. Picks come from S&P 500 members only, each counted only while it was in the index (the real daily member lists, 1996 on). Former members are priced where data exists, from Tiingo when Yahoo no longer carries them: 56% of members in 2000, 82% in 2010 and 97% since 2020. Most of the rest went bankrupt or were bought out before 2010, so the early years are still somewhat flattered; results from 2010 on rest on nearly complete data. Small caps are deliberately excluded: adding the Russell 2000 cut the result to about +509% with a −73% drawdown.
      • Risk. Five stocks is concentrated: in the backtest since 2000 the stocks alone, never stepping aside, fell as much as −85%, and the default plan, with its moves into gold and bonds, −35%. It trailed QQQ in some years, and a single year's gains can come mostly from one theme. Prices from Yahoo Finance, split-adjusted closes (benchmarks include dividends). A mechanical rule's output, not investment advice.
